mcqs.question: What's the concrete mechanism behind "make this endpoint idempotent"?
options: The client generates an idempotency key, the server stores the key with its result, and dedupes on retry
The server simply logs every request and hopes duplicates don't matter
The client retries with a brand-new random key each time to avoid collisions
The server ignores retries entirely and always reprocesses the request
mcqs.explanation: Idempotency needs an actual mechanism: a key generated once per logical request, stored server-side with the result, checked before any side-effecting work runs. Logging without deduping, generating a new key per retry, or reprocessing every request all fail to prevent the duplicate side effect.

mcqs.question: For the payment endpoint's idempotency key to work, what must the client do on retry?
options: A new idempotency key must be generated for every retry of the same charge attempt
The client resends the same idempotency key on every retry of the same logical charge attempt
The server generates the idempotency key and sends it back to the client
The dedup store only needs to keep keys for a few seconds
mcqs.explanation: The whole mechanism depends on the retry carrying the identical key as the original attempt, so the server can recognize it as the same logical request. A new key per retry defeats deduplication, the client (not the server) generates the key, and a TTL of a few seconds is usually too short for realistic retry windows.

mcqs.question: What's the real trade-off in adding idempotency-key handling to an endpoint?
options: It has no cost at all — it should be added to every endpoint unconditionally
It eliminates the need for a database entirely
It adds a lookup and a write to the dedup store on every request, worth it exactly where retries are actually expected
It only works for GET requests
mcqs.explanation: Every request now pays a lookup-and-write cost against the dedup store — real but usually small, and worth paying on endpoints reachable by retries. It's not free, doesn't remove the need for a database, and applies to any side-effecting endpoint, not just GETs (which rarely need it since they have no side effects to duplicate).

mcqs.question: Why can't you assume a PUT endpoint is automatically safe to retry just because PUT is 'idempotent'?
options: PUT requests never have side effects
Idempotent HTTP verbs are enforced automatically by web servers
A PUT can never be retried safely under any circumstances
The HTTP verb being conventionally idempotent doesn't guarantee the handler's actual implementation is safe to repeat, e.g. an increment inside a PUT
mcqs.explanation: The verb describes intended semantics, not an implementation guarantee — a PUT handler that increments a balance instead of setting it repeats that side effect on every retry regardless of the verb. Web servers don't enforce this automatically, and a well-implemented PUT can absolutely be retried safely.
